back: Two different metals in an electrolyte, joined by a wire; it changes chemical energy into electrical energy.

front: Which metal is the negative electrode of a simple cell?
back: The more reactive metal: it loses electrons more readily (e.g. zinc in a zinc–copper cell).

front: Reaction at the zinc electrode of a zinc–copper cell
Reaction at the copper electrode in dilute acid
back: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (bubbles of hydrogen on the copper).

front: What decides the voltage of a simple cell?
back: How far apart the two metals are in the reactivity series: further apart, bigger voltage; same metal, 0 V.
Two or more cells joined together, e.g. six 2 V cells in a 12 V car battery.
Negative: spongy lead. Positive: lead(IV) oxide. Electrolyte: dilute sulfuric acid.

front: Overall reaction as a lead-acid battery discharges
What happens when a lead-acid battery is charged?
back: A current is forced through it the other way: PbSO₄ changes back to Pb and PbO₂; electrical energy is stored as chemical energy.
Top up with distilled water; clean, greased terminals; recharge promptly; recycle when worn out.

front: Why charge a battery in a ventilated place with no flames?
back: Water is electrolysed near full charge, giving hydrogen and oxygen, which can explode.
